image.altEn: Spanish-language xkcd comic #705: Devotion to Duty

titleText.es: El extraño sentido del deber que tienen los buenos sysadmins bordea lo sociopático, pero está bien saber que se interpone entre las fuerzas de la oscuridad y los servidores del blog de tu gato.
titleText.en: The weird sense of duty really good sysadmins have can border on the sociopathic, but it's nice to know that it stands between the forces of darkness and your cat blog's servers.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive and official xkcd source both identify comic #705, published 2010-02-22, and their title texts are preserved exactly. The Spanish raster integrates the technical loans UPTIME and SYSADMIN into Spanish syntax, so both remain lexical targets. OCR split the printed wraps ASEGURA-/DO, COR-/TADO, COMUNICACIO-/NES, VENTILA-/CIÓN, MUR-/MURANDO, and TRATA-/MOS; misread IGNORÓ as INGORÓ and the second part of MURMURANDO as ELRANDO; and entirely omitted the separate EL and quoted UPTIME line. The authored transcript follows the visible raster rather than those OCR errors.

regions.labelEs: HEMOS CAPTURADO A LOS REHENES, ASEGURADO EL EDIFICIO Y CORTADO LAS COMUNICACIONES, COMO DIJISTE.

applications.explanationEn: Hemos supplies the present helper for nosotros, and capturado names the first completed action.
Asegurado is a second completed action coordinated under the earlier shared helper hemos.
Cortado is a third completed action coordinated under the earlier shared helper hemos.
A marks the specific people as the direct object, and los rehenes supplies the complete person group.
Cortado supplies the completed action, and las comunicaciones names the links or systems that were cut off.
Como refers back to the earlier instruction, and dijiste identifies what one familiar listener said.
Dijiste presents the earlier act of saying as one completed event.

regions.labelEs: PERO LUEGO ESTE TIPO TREPÓ POR LOS CONDUCTOS DE VENTILACIÓN Y ATRAVESÓ CRISTALES ROTOS, MATANDO A TODOS LOS QUE ENVIAMOS PARA DETENERLE.

applications.exampleEs: TREPÓ POR LOS CONDUCTOS DE VENTILACIÓN
applications.explanationEn: Trepó supplies the completed climb, por introduces its route, and los conductos de ventilación fills that route slot.
Conductos names the passages, and de ventilación identifies their function while ventilación remains singular.
Rotos follows cristales in the common neutral order for a descriptive adjective.
Rotos uses masculine plural -os to match masculine plural cristales.
Matando adds an action happening alongside the movement through the broken glass.
A marks the defined group of people as the direct object, and todos los que enviamos supplies that complete group.
Todos los identifies an understood group of people, and que introduces the action enviamos that defines them.
Los identifies an unnamed masculine or mixed group, que introduces what defines that group, and enviamos supplies the defining action.
Para introduces the purpose, and detenerle keeps detener in its unchanged -er form with the person word attached.
Le is written on the end of the unchanged verb detener as one word.
Trepó presents the climb as one bounded completed event.
Atravesó presents the crossing as one bounded completed event.
Enviamos presents the dispatch of other people as a completed event in the report.
Ha rescatado is the finite core of the question. Spanish keeps the statement order and uses the surrounding question marks and intonation rather than adding a separate helper word.
Ha matches one person, and rescatado supplies the completed rescue whose result matters now.
A marks the specific people as the direct object, and los rehenes supplies the complete group.

regions.labelEs: NO, LOS IGNORÓ. SOLO RECONECTÓ LOS CABLES QUE CORTAMOS, MURMURANDO ALGO SOBRE EL "UPTIME".

applications.explanationEn: Los represents the masculine plural people and appears before the changed verb ignoró.
Cables is the thing described, que links it to the description, and cortamos states what the speakers did to those cables.
Murmurando adds the quiet speech happening while the person reconnects the cables.
Murmurando supplies the quiet speech, algo leaves its content vague, and sobre el uptime fills the topic slot.
Ignoró presents ignoring the people as one bounded completed event.
Reconectó presents reconnecting the cables as one bounded completed event.
Cortamos is the same shape in present and completed-past time; this completed narrative gives it the earlier finished-action reading.
Tratamos names the ongoing situation, con introduces what the speakers face, and un sysadmin fills that slot.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.noteEn: Capturado is the completed-action form of capturar. After a form of haber, it describes the completed act of capturing someone or something.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks a specific person as the object
cards.noteEn: Spanish generally places a before a specific person who receives a verb’s action. This “personal a” is not translated as a separate English word.

cards.promptEs: a + persona o expresión que se refiere a una persona
cards.questionEn: Why does Spanish sometimes put a before the person affected by an action?
cards.answerEn: Put a before a person—or a word such as alguien or nadie—when that person directly receives the action.
cards.noteEn: This a is called the personal a. It is common before a named or specific person, but person-denoting words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) also take it. English usually has no separate word for it. Before the masculine article el, a + el contracts to al.
Rehenes is the plural of rehén, a person held so that another person or group will meet a demand.
Asegurado is the completed-action form of asegurar. In a security context it can mean bringing a place under control or making it safe.

example.es: El equipo ha asegurado la entrada.
example.en: The team has secured the entrance.

cards.noteEn: Cortado is the completed-action form of cortar. With a service, signal, or communication link, it means that the connection has been interrupted.

example.es: Han cortado la conexión durante la reparación.
example.en: They have cut off the connection during the repair.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that communication links are cut off?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of cortar followed by las comunicaciones.
cards.noteEn: Cortar changes for the person and time. Las comunicaciones names the channels or systems that are interrupted.
Comunicaciones can refer collectively to the systems or channels used to exchange messages and information.

example.en: The storm damaged the communications systems.

cards.noteEn: Unaccented como can introduce the person, thing, or situation used for a comparison. It does not ask “how”; the question word cómo has an accent.

cards.questionEn: How can you refer back to something one familiar listener said?
cards.answerEn: Say como dijiste, meaning ‘as you said.’
cards.noteEn: Como introduces the comparison with the earlier words, and dijiste is the completed-past tú form of decir. Other people require a different form: como dije, como dijo, como dijimos.

example.en: I did it as you said.

cards.noteEn: Dijiste is decir's completed-past form for one person addressed informally. Its stem changes from dec- to dij-.

cards.answerEn: Use the preterite for a completed event and the imperfect for background, an ongoing situation, or something that used to happen.
cards.noteEn: Think of a story: the preterite answers “What happened next?” The imperfect answers “What was happening?”, “What were things like?”, or “What used to happen?” These two names describe how the speaker presents an event, not simply how long it lasted.
cards.questionEn: Spanish has two common ways to talk about the past. When do you use each one?

example.en: While I was walking, it started to rain.

cards.noteEn: Excelente can describe something of very high quality or stand alone as a positive reaction to news or a result.
In informal speech, tipo can refer to a man as “guy.” In other contexts, it can instead mean a type or kind.
Trepó is the completed-past form of trepar for one person or thing. It presents the climb as a finished event.

example.es: El gato trepó por el árbol.
example.en: The cat climbed up the tree.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone climbs through, along, or up a route or surface?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of trepar, then por, then name the route or surface.
cards.noteEn: Trepar changes for the person and time. Por introduces the path used for the climb.

example.es: Trepamos por la pared de roca.
example.en: We climbed up the rock wall.

cards.answerEn: through; along; down; via (a movement path)
cards.noteEn: Por can mark the path followed during movement. English may choose through, along, down, or via according to the route.
A conducto is an enclosed channel through which air, liquid, cables, or another material can pass. Conductos is plural.

example.es: El aire circula por los conductos.
example.en: The air circulates through the ducts.

cards.questionEn: What is a common Spanish expression for a ventilation duct?
cards.answerEn: Say conducto de ventilación; use conductos de ventilación in the plural.
cards.noteEn: Conducto names the passage, while de ventilación identifies its function. Ventilación stays singular after de.

cards.answerEn: often no separate English word; links a noun to another noun that names its type or use
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between two nouns where English uses a noun directly before another noun. For example, una taza de café is ‘a coffee cup,’ and material de oficina is ‘office material.’
Ventilación is the movement or replacement of air in an enclosed space.
Atravesó is the completed-past form of atravesar for one person or thing. It describes movement from one side of something to the other.
Cristal can mean glass as a material or one pane or panel of glass. Cristales is plural.

example.es: Cambiaron los cristales de las ventanas.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.noteEn: Rotos is the masculine plural form of roto. It matches a masculine plural noun describing things that have broken.
Matando is the -ando form of matar. It can add an action that happens at the same time as another action.

example.es: El veneno avanzó, matando a los insectos.
example.en: The poison spread, killing the insects.

cards.promptEs: -ando / -iendo para una acción simultánea o un medio
cards.questionEn: How can you add an action that happens at the same time or explains how something is done?
cards.answerEn: Use the action form ending in -ando or -iendo, such as hablando or corriendo.
cards.noteEn: Spanish calls this form the gerund. It does not change for the person. Used on its own, it can describe a simultaneous action or the means used: Entró corriendo means the person entered by running. This differs from estar plus the same form, which focuses on an action in progress.

cards.questionEn: How do you add information about a named person or thing using “who,” “that,” or “which”?
cards.answerEn: Put que after the person or thing, then add a verb and the information about it.
cards.noteEn: Que links the added description to the person or thing before it. It does not change for masculine, feminine, singular, or plural nouns. The added part needs a verb: la casa que vimos means “the house that we saw.”

example.es: La casa que vimos es azul.
example.en: The house that we saw is blue.

cards.answerEn: those; the ones (as part of los que)
cards.noteEn: Los normally means “the” before a masculine plural noun. In los que followed by a description, the noun is left unstated and los identifies a masculine or mixed group: los que llegaron means “those who arrived.”

example.es: Conozco a los que viven aquí.
example.en: I know those who live here.

cards.questionEn: How do you say ‘the one who…’ or ‘the ones that…’ without repeating the noun?
cards.answerEn: Use el que, la que, los que, or las que to match the unnamed person or thing, then add what identifies it.
cards.noteEn: Choose el, la, los, or las to show whether the omitted person or thing is masculine or feminine, singular or plural. Que stays unchanged and introduces the identifying description, which normally contains a verb. Each plus sign in the prompt means ‘followed by.’

example.es: Ana es la que prepara el café.
example.en: Ana is the one who makes the coffee.

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.noteEn: Enviamos can be present or completed past. A narrative of finished events gives it the completed-past reading.

cards.answerEn: Use para followed by the verb’s dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Use para + verb when the same person or thing performs both actions: in estudio para aprender, I both study and learn. When someone else performs the second action, Spanish needs the different pattern para que.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “in order to do something” in Spanish?

example.en: I study in order to learn.

cards.noteEn: Detener stays in its unchanged -er form and le is attached to represent a male person. This use of le for a singular male person is common and accepted in Spain; detenerlo is also widely used.

example.es: Mandaron a dos agentes para detenerle.
example.en: They sent two officers to stop him.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

cards.questionEn: How can Spanish turn an ordinary statement into a yes-or-no question?
cards.answerEn: Use question marks and questioning intonation; Spanish does not need a separate helper like English do or does.
cards.noteEn: The word order can remain the same as in a statement, especially in conversation. The opening and closing question marks show the question in writing.
Rescatado is the completed-action form of rescatar. After a form of haber, it describes a completed rescue.

cards.answerEn: A system administrator maintains services and may care intensely about uptime, the time those services remain available.
cards.noteEn: The joke makes that professional duty absurdly dominant: the intruder ignores hostages and danger, restores the cut cables, and is recognized as a sysadmin because he prioritizes uptime above the ostensible rescue mission.

cards.promptEs: lo, la, los, las delante de un verbo conjugado
cards.questionEn: Where do you put the Spanish word for “it” or “them” when the main verb already shows who acts and when?
cards.answerEn: Put lo, la, los, or las directly before that verb.
cards.noteEn: These short words replace the person or thing directly affected by the action; that role is called the direct object. Choose lo or los for a masculine thing, la or las for a feminine thing, and match singular or plural. Before a verb form such as conté or vimos, write the short word separately in front: lo conté, las vimos. With an unchanged dictionary form, it can instead attach to the end, as in verlo.
Ignoró is the completed-past form of ignorar for one person or thing. The written accent distinguishes this form from present-time ignoro, ‘I ignore.’
Reconectó is the completed-past form of reconectar for one person or thing. The prefix re- adds the sense of connecting again.

cards.answerEn: we cut off; we discontinue; we cut off (completed past)
cards.noteEn: Cortamos is the nosotros form of cortar in both the present and the completed past. With a service, supply, cable, or connection, cortar can mean stopping or disconnecting it rather than literally slicing it; context shows the time intended.

example.es: Ayer cortamos el servicio durante una hora.
example.en: Yesterday we cut off the service for an hour.

cards.noteEn: Murmurando is the -ando form of murmurar. It describes speaking very quietly or indistinctly while another action happens.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone quietly mutters something about a topic?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of murmurar, optionally add algo, then use sobre before the topic.
cards.noteEn: Murmurar changes for the person and time. Sobre introduces what the quiet remark concerns.

example.en: She muttered something about the schedule.

cards.answerEn: uptime; time a system remains available
cards.noteEn: Uptime is an English technical loan used by Spanish-speaking computing professionals for the time that a computer or service stays running and reachable.

example.es: El servidor mantiene un uptime muy alto.
example.en: The server maintains very high uptime.

cards.answerEn: we are dealing; we deal (with con)
cards.noteEn: Tratamos is the present nosotros form of tratar. Followed by con, it can mean dealing with or facing a person, problem, or situation.

example.en: We are dealing with a delicate problem.

cards.promptEs: tratar con + persona, problema o situación
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone deals with or faces a person, problem, or situation?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of tratar followed by con and the person or thing.
cards.noteEn: Tratar changes for the person and time, while con stays unchanged before what is being dealt with.

example.es: La directora trata con muchos proveedores.
example.en: The director deals with many suppliers.

cards.noteEn: Sysadmin is an English computing loan used for the person who maintains computer systems, servers, accounts, and related services. Spanish also uses administrador or administradora de sistemas.

example.en: The system administrator checked the servers.
